account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on 8 June 2026, or 3:33 a.m. on 9 June in Oman. That time marks the rescue and is distinct from the time that the helicopter went down. Central Command said that both were rescued within approximately two hours and that they were stable. Its release said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew and carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. Al-Monitor reported on 10 June 2026 that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the Corsair from afar. Stars and Stripes reported the same day that the vessel was guided to the site, located the soldiers and carried them to safer waters. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies told the paper that a drone gives the same capability at less risk than a crewed platform. The sources do not identify which functions of the vessel ran on their own during the rescue. On 18 September 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Saronic employees that the pilots are alive because of the vessel. No finding on the cause of the helicopter's loss has been published.

ai_role.statement: Hawkins identified an unmanned Corsair as the recovery vessel. Al-Monitor reported that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the vessel from afar. Stars and Stripes reported that the Corsair was guided to the site, located the soldiers and carried them to safer waters. No source states which functions ran on their own or what the vessel's sensors contributed. A crewed helicopter completed the recovery.

fields.account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on 8 June 2026, or 3:33 a.m. on 9 June in Oman. That time marks the rescue and is distinct from the time that the helicopter went down. Central Command said that both were rescued within approximately two hours and that they were stable. Its release said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew and carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. Al-Monitor reported on 10 June 2026 that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the Corsair from afar. Stars and Stripes reported the same day that the vessel was guided to the site, located the soldiers and carried them to safer waters. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies told the paper that a drone gives the same capability at less risk than a crewed platform. The sources do not identify which functions of the vessel ran on their own during the rescue. On 18 September 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Saronic employees that the pilots are alive because of the vessel. No finding on the cause of the helicopter's loss has been published.
fields.summary: A remotely piloted Saronic Corsair sea drone carried two Apache crew off Oman to a helicopter hoist; Central Command reported that both were rescued within approximately two hours.

display.answer: The vessel was unmanned, but the sources do not establish the navigation mode or which decisions were autonomous during this rescue. Human-supervised operation is the most likely arrangement.
display.editor_note: The named naval unit operated the vessel and coordinated a helicopter transfer; platform capability alone cannot establish unattended decision-making.

purpose: The Corsair is an autonomous maritime platform that Task Force 59 had been fielding since late March 2026. In this case, the military used it to carry stranded crew members to a helicopter recovery point.

ratings.reason: Two aviators were recovered from the water and transferred to a helicopter within approximately two hours, according to U.S. Central Command. Their condition was stable. The sources do not establish the risk of death without the rescue or whether another rescue asset could have reached them.

No source reports a realized outcome for the military beyond the recovery of the two crew members, and the lower risk to crewed rescuers rests on an analyst's general statement, so the extent of any benefit to the organization cannot be established.
